short: British codebreakers at Bletchley Park operationalised Colossus, the world's first programmable, electronic, digital computer, to decipher German communications.
full:
On 5 February 1944, the Colossus Mark I carried out its first successful cryptanalytic attack at Bletchley Park, reading high-level teleprinter messages encrypted by the German Lorenz SZ40/42 machine. Designed by Post Office engineer Tommy Flowers, the machine used over 1,500 vacuum tubes to perform Boolean operations and rapidly simulate the mechanical rotors of the German cipher system. This electronic approach replaced significantly slower electro-mechanical methods, reducing the time required to read a message from weeks to hours.

Ten Colossus machines were built by the end of the war, providing Allied commanders with vital strategic intelligence, including confirmation that the German high command had been deceived about the location of the D-Day landings. Because its existence remained highly classified for decades, Colossus was omitted from the early history of computing hardware. However, it stands as a fundamental milestone that proved the viability of large-scale electronic data processing.
